title: Design an LLM Inference Serving Gateway
prompt: Design an inference gateway that serves large language models to many internal teams and external customers. It must multiplex requests across a GPU fleet with continuous batching and KV-cache management, route between models with fallback, stream tokens, enforce per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and keep GPU cost under control. Assume bursty, heterogeneous traffic and strict latency SLOs.
blurb: The GPU-serving control plane — continuous batching, KV cache, autoscaling, routing/fallback, streaming, rate limits, and cost.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (route, batch, stream, fallback, quota) from non-functional (TTFT and inter-token latency SLOs, throughput, availability, cost per 1M tokens).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about model sizes/mix, prompt vs generation length distribution, tenant SLO tiers, sync vs streaming, on-prem vs cloud GPUs, and cost targets.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Estimates tokens/s per GPU, KV-cache memory per request (layers x heads x dim x 2 x seq x dtype), max concurrent sequences per GPU, GPUs needed for peak QPS, and cost per 1M tokens.

rubric.label: Continuous batching
rubric.description: Continuous/in-flight batching vs static batching, prefill vs decode separation, scheduling to keep GPUs saturated without hurting TTFT.

rubric.label: KV cache management
rubric.description: KV-cache memory budgeting, paged attention, eviction/preemption under pressure, prefix caching for shared system prompts.

rubric.label: Routing & fallback
rubric.description: Model/version routing, health-aware load balancing, fallback to alternate replicas/models/regions on overload or failure, and graceful degradation.

rubric.label: GPU autoscaling
rubric.description: Scaling on queue depth/GPU utilization rather than CPU, cold-start (model load) mitigation, warm pools, scale-to-zero tradeoffs for expensive GPUs.

rubric.label: Rate limiting & quotas
rubric.description: Token-bucket limits by requests and by tokens, per-tenant quotas, fair queueing, admission control and backpressure under overload.

rubric.label: Streaming & protocol
rubric.description: SSE/gRPC streaming, cancellation freeing GPU slots, TTFT vs inter-token latency, timeouts and partial-response handling.

rubric.label: Cost efficiency
rubric.description: Maximizing tokens/GPU-hour via batching and quantization, spot/preemptible GPUs, semantic/prefix caching, right-sizing models per request.

rubric.label: ML serving specifics
rubric.description: Quantization (INT8/FP8) and tensor/pipeline parallelism tradeoffs, speculative decoding, prefix-cache reuse, model versioning and canary.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: TTFT/ITL/throughput SLOs, GPU utilization and KV-cache occupancy, queue depth, per-tenant token accounting, and cost dashboards.

functional_requirements: Accept chat/completion requests and route to the right model/version
Batch concurrent requests across the GPU fleet efficiently
Stream tokens back with cancellation support
Fall back across replicas/models/regions on overload or failure
Enforce per-tenant rate limits and token quotas
nonfunctional_requirements: High GPU utilization / low cost per 1M tokens
High availability with graceful degradation under overload
Isolation so one noisy tenant can't starve others
clarifying_questions: Which models and sizes, and what's the request mix across them?
Distribution of prompt length vs generation length?
Tenant SLO tiers and quotas — do we oversubscribe?
Owned GPUs, cloud on-demand, or spot/preemptible? Cost target per 1M tokens?
Do we serve one prompt template widely (prefix-cache opportunity)?
qualifying_questions: Do we need multi-region for latency/residency?
Are function-calling/tool schemas and structured outputs in scope?

estimations.throughput: A single large model on one high-memory GPU sustains order 1-3k output tokens/s aggregate with continuous batching (workload-dependent)
estimations.kv_cache_per_req: KV bytes ≈ 2 x layers x hidden x seq_len x dtype_bytes; a few hundred MB to low GBs per long sequence — this caps concurrent sequences
estimations.concurrency: Max concurrent sequences ≈ (GPU mem − weights) / KV-per-seq; long contexts sharply reduce it
estimations.fleet_sizing: GPUs ≈ peak output tokens/s ÷ tokens/s-per-GPU, plus headroom for prefill spikes and failover
estimations.cost: Cost/1M tokens = GPU $/hr ÷ (tokens/s-per-GPU x 3600 x utilization); batching + quantization move this the most

core_components: API gateway / edge (auth, rate limit, admission control)
Router / scheduler (model selection, load-aware balancing, fallback)
Per-model inference servers (continuous batching engine, e.g. paged-attention style)
data_model: models(model_id, version, engine, gpu_type, parallelism, quantization, weights_uri, status)
usage(request_id, tenant_id, model_id, prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, ttft_ms, ts)
api_design: POST /v1/chat/completions { model, messages, stream, max_tokens } → SSE token stream { delta, finish_reason }
Client cancel (disconnect) → free the sequence's KV slot immediately
429 with Retry-After + rate-limit headers on quota exhaustion
reference.high_level_design: Request hits the edge: authenticate, check token-bucket rate limits (by RPM and TPM) and quota, then admission control (reject/queue if the target model pool is saturated). The router picks a model version and a healthy replica by load (queue depth, KV occupancy). The inference server runs continuous/in-flight batching: new requests join the running batch at the next decode step, prefill and decode are scheduled to keep the GPU busy without starving TTFT. The KV-cache manager pages attention memory, reuses shared prefixes (system prompts), and preempts/evicts the lowest-priority sequences under memory pressure. Tokens stream back via SSE; cancellation frees the KV slot. The autoscaler scales GPU replicas on queue depth/utilization with a warm pool to hide model-load cold starts. Usage is metered per tenant for quotas and billing; overload degrades gracefully via fallback chains and load shedding of low-tier traffic.

deep_dives.probe: Static batching wastes GPU when sequences finish at different times. Explain continuous/in-flight batching — how do new requests join mid-flight, and how do you balance prefill spikes against decode TTFT?
The KV cache fills up and you can't admit more sequences. Walk me through paged attention, prefix reuse for shared system prompts, and what you evict or preempt under pressure.
GPU cold start (loading tens of GB of weights) is slow. How do you autoscale on the right signal and hide cold starts — warm pools, scale-to-zero economics?
A model replica is overloaded or a region degrades. What's your fallback chain, and how do you avoid retry storms making it worse?
Rate limiting by request count is wrong for LLMs. How do you limit by tokens (TPM), enforce fairness across tenants, and apply backpressure without hurting TTFT?
Your cost per 1M tokens is too high. Which levers — batching, quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, spot GPUs — do you pull and what do they cost you?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions kv cache or cache or prefix cache
followup_bank.question: How is the KV cache / prefix cache evicted when GPU memory is exhausted — LRU by sequence, priority-based preemption, recompute-on-demand? And how do you avoid thrashing?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions semantic cache or response cache or embeddings
followup_bank.question: For a semantic cache of responses, how do you keep it fresh (invalidate when the model version or system prompt changes), and what's the eviction policy?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions database or registry or postgres
followup_bank.question: Model registry and usage records live in a datastore — how do you propagate a new model version or quota change to the fleet, CDC vs config push?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions autoscaling or kubernetes or scale
followup_bank.question: What metric do you autoscale on for GPUs, and how do you handle multi-minute cold starts without SLO violations?

scaling: Horizontal replicas per model behind a load-aware router
Tensor/pipeline parallelism to fit large models across GPUs
Disaggregated prefill vs decode pools to isolate their very different profiles
Multi-region with locality routing and cross-region failover
Warm pools + predictive scaling for diurnal traffic
bottlenecks: KV-cache memory caps concurrency, especially for long contexts
Prefill of long prompts spikes latency and steals decode cycles
Head-of-line blocking / unfair queueing under overload
Retry storms amplifying a partial outage
tradeoffs: Bigger batches (throughput/cost) vs TTFT and tail latency
Quantization (more throughput, cheaper) vs small quality loss
Scale-to-zero (cost) vs cold-start latency for expensive GPUs
Speculative decoding (lower latency) vs extra compute and complexity
Oversubscribing quotas (utilization) vs SLO risk under bursts
alternative_solutions: Managed model-API providers instead of self-hosting (less control, per-token cost)
Per-team dedicated GPU deployments (isolation but poor utilization)
Offline/batch inference queue for non-interactive workloads
Model distillation to a smaller model to cut serving cost
observability: TTFT, inter-token latency, and throughput SLOs per model/tenant
GPU utilization, KV-cache occupancy, batch size, queue depth
Per-tenant token accounting and quota consumption
Cost per 1M tokens dashboard and per-tenant chargeback
security: Per-tenant auth, isolation, and quota enforcement
Input/output guardrails and PII handling in the gateway
Prevent prompt-leakage of shared prefix-cached system prompts across tenants
Audit logging of requests for compliance
mTLS between gateway and inference servers
reference.reference_answer: A strong staff-level answer starts from SLOs (TTFT, inter-token latency) and cost per 1M tokens, then estimates tokens/s per GPU and KV-cache memory per sequence to size concurrency and the fleet. It designs a control plane — edge auth + token-based (TPM) rate limiting + admission control → load-aware router with fallback chains → inference servers doing continuous/in-flight batching with paged-attention KV management and prefix reuse. It handles overload with backpressure, load shedding of low tiers, and retry-storm avoidance; autoscales GPUs on queue depth with warm pools to hide cold starts; and pulls explicit cost levers (batching, quantization, speculative decoding, prefix/semantic caching, spot GPUs). It calls out KV-cache memory and prefill spikes as the core bottlenecks, streams with cancellation that frees GPU slots, and meters tokens per tenant for quotas and billing.

interviewer_notes: This is a staff question — expect the candidate to reason quantitatively about GPU memory and KV cache, not just draw boxes. The two highest-signal deep dives are continuous batching and KV-cache management; if they only know static batching or ignore KV memory as the concurrency limiter, that caps the score. Push the rate-limiting probe until they limit by tokens (TPM), not just requests. Use the KV/prefix-cache eviction follow-up and the autoscaling cold-start follow-up as interrupts. Strong candidates separate prefill from decode, reason about TTFT vs throughput tradeoffs of batch size, and treat cost per 1M tokens as a first-class SLO with concrete levers. Reserve time for graceful degradation under overload — retry storms and fair queueing separate staff from senior.
